description: co-Astronauts is a student research team exploring the intersection of space science and medicine. We’re interested in how radiation and other factors during long-duration space missions may affect overall health. We aim to use NASA data and existing research to develop a computational health-monitoring system.
summary: Space environments expose astronauts to radiation, microgravity, and prolonged isolation, making it difficult to detect and diagnose biological side effects in orbit. To address this, we developed ARES-74 × Co-Astronauts, a health-monitoring web platform tailored for both short-duration and long-duration space missions. The platform integrates personal crew biometric telemetry, vital-check renewal reminders, circadian rhythm and sleep tracking, a PIN-protected AI support chat (AURA), 4-7-8 breathing and Earth sensory audio tools, color-coded (Green/Amber/Red) health guidance, and a guide for spotting breakdowns across 30 medical devices. Alongside personal vitals, the dashboard monitors habitat conditions—including cabin pressure, temperature, O₂ and CO₂ gas levels, and live space weather and radiation alerts from NASA and NOAA feeds—helping astronauts diagnose health risks early. Built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, a Node.js and Express backend, and the Web Audio API, the project models realistic spaceflight scenarios while prioritizing practical, intuitive usability when real-time medical support from Earth is delayed.
details:
ARES-74 × Co-Astronauts: An Integrated Astronaut Health Monitoring, Medical Guidance and Crew Wellbeing Platform

ARES-74 × Co-Astronauts is an integrated health and crew support platform designed to support astronaut health, wellbeing and operational safety throughout a mission. Acknowledging the fact that human spaceflight involves an interplay of physiological, psychological and environmental factors the platform integrates astronaut health monitoring, spacecraft environmental data, medical guidance, psychological support and biomedical equipment data into a single accessible interface.

Comprehensive Physiological Health Monitoring

The platform provides a neurophysiological dashboard for monitoring a range of key health parameters: heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV) sleep, recovery, oxygen saturation (Spo2) physical strain and radiation exposure. It also includes health parameters associated with the risks identified by NASAs Human Research Program (HRP) namely Spaceflight Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS) bone mineral density, renal stone risk, muscle loss orthostatic intolerance, vestibular dysfunction, immune change, core body temperature, microbiome and decompression risk during EVAs. It also has a number of parameters that relate to teaming, nutrition and hydration to give a more complete picture of crew health.

Spacecraft Environment and Space Weather Monitoring

Astronaut health can't be assessed in any way without reference to the environment in which the crew is operating. ARES-74 therefore includes an environmental monitoring interface which covers ISS cabin pressure, cabin O2 and CO2 concentrations cabin temperature orbital altitude, solar exposure and space weather. Its NASA telemetry interface is set up to pull data from the ISS live data streams the data, the GOES proton flux and the NASA DONKI space weather alert systems. The environmental data is of course a complement to the physiological monitoring and enables the astronaut to get a sense of the external factors that may be affecting them.

Health Guidance and Risk Awareness

A key component of ARES-74 is the Health Guidance Encyclopedia which categorises the 15 health conditions and associated guidance entries into three levels: Green (optimal) Amber (caution) and Red (critical). This enables the astronaut to assess the significance of any health change understand the relevant spaceflight related physiological mechanisms and know what to do next. The concept is to take the medical and space medicine information and present it in a way that is easily digestible and to support the astronaut in making informed health related decisions thereby reducing their reliance on a piecemeal approach to medical information (particularly when there is a communications lag).

Psychological Wellbeing and Confidential Crew Support

Long duration missions involve isolation, confinement, separation from family and the kinds of demands that can have an impact on psychological wellbeing and cognitive performance. ARES-74 addresses this aspect via a psychological check-in whereby the astronaut can report whether they are feeling calm and rested, stressed or anxious or exhausted and in a state of psychological distress.

The platform also features AURA Care, an AI assisted support interface with dedicated roles for a psychologist, flight surgeon and operations copilot. It's a point of contact for a range of crew support needs. There's a PIN protected interface for use and a range of wellbeing features including a 4 7 8 guided breathing pacer and a range of relaxing soundscapes to provide simple tools for stress management and emotional regulation.

Maintaining Emotional Connection with Earth

Recognising the importance of connection during the long isolation of a space mission, the Loved Ones Voice Recordings feature allows the astronaut to record or upload voice messages from family, partner and friends. These can be listened to during the mission. Are an important way of maintaining the emotional connection with people on Earth. It's a feature that underlines the fact that astronaut wellbeing's much more than just the physiological parameters. It's about resilience it's about social support and its about having a sense of connection.

Biomedical Equipment and Operational Safety

ARES-74 also contains a diagnostic guidebook covering 30 of the more commonly used spaceflight medical devices and their potential malfunction indicators. This is designed to assist the crew in identifying equipment abnormalities and in understanding the information associated with them. There is a biomedical measurement reminder system for the measurements (heart rate, radiation dosimetry, Spo2 blood pressure, body temperature etc.). A dedicated anomaly reporting interface which allows the crew to report any suspicious biomedical equipment conditions and then dispatch the report via the NASA CHeCS anomaly dispatch interface.

NASA Open Data Integration and Data Accessibility

The platform has a NASA data integration interface which supports telemetry links and the import of CSV data from a range of sources including NASAs Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). Nasas public data catalogue. This allows for the use of available spaceflight research data and for the platform to be extended with further data sets. It's a platform which brings together physiological data, environmental data and health guidance in a single interface.

A Holistic Approach to Human Spaceflight Health

The key contribution of ARES-74 × Co-Astronauts is its approach to astronaut care. It doesn't treat signs spaceflight health risks, the environment, psychological wellbeing and the biomedical equipment as discrete issues. It brings them all together to give a holistic view of crew health and mission safety.

By combining monitoring, environmental awareness readily available medical information, psychological support, social connection and operational resources ARES-74 is designed to enhance astronaut autonomy and support more effective health management during missions where access to Earth-based medical support may be very limited.

Ultimately ARES-74 × Co-Astronauts is a more connected human-centred approach to spaceflight health supporting the physical safety of the astronaut as well as their psychological resilience, autonomy and general wellbeing throughout the journey, beyond Earth.
